title: HMMT — Random Mock #1
instructions: 7 questions · 35 minutes · No calculator. Proof-based problems: write full solutions, then compare with the official solutions.

questions.source: Modified from 2022 HMMT November General Problem 1
questions.question: Emily's broken clock runs backwards at three times the speed of a regular clock. Right now, it is displaying the wrong time. How many times will it display the correct time in the next $24$ hours? (It is an analog clock.)
questions.solution: The displayed time drifts backward at 3x while real time advances at 1x, so the gap closes at 4x. The clock is correct whenever the gap is a multiple of 12 hours: $4t \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$, i.e. $t = 3, 6, \dots, 24$ — $8$ times.

questions.source: Modified from 2022 HMMT November Theme Problem 2
questions.question: Alice is thinking of a positive real number $x$, and Bob is thinking of a positive real number $y$. Given that $x\sqrt{y} = 8$ and $(\sqrt{x})^{y} = 16$, compute $xy$.
questions.solution: From $x\sqrt{y} = 8$, we get $x = 8/\sqrt{y}$. Substituting into $(\sqrt{x})^{y} = 16$: trying $y = 4$ gives $x = 4$, and indeed $4\sqrt{4} = 8$ and $(\sqrt{4})^4 = 16$. Hence $xy = 16$.

questions.source: Modified from 2023 HMMT November General Problem 2
questions.question: A regular $n$-gon $P_1 P_2 \ldots P_n$ satisfies $\angle P_1 P_7 P_8 = 176^{\circ}$. Compute $n$.
questions.solution: Let $O$ be the center. The arc from $P_1$ to $P_8$ not containing $P_7$ has central angle $2(180^{\circ} - 176^{\circ}) = 8^{\circ}$. This arc spans 7 sides, so $7 \cdot \frac{360^{\circ}}{n} = 8^{\circ}$, giving $n = 315$.

questions.source: Modified from 2023 HMMT November General Problem 3
questions.question: Compute the number of positive four-digit multiples of $11$ whose sum of digits (in base ten) is divisible by $3$.
questions.solution: Direct enumeration: there are $818$ four-digit multiples of $11$ (from $1001$ to $9999$... precisely $\lfloor 9999/11 \rfloor - \lfloor 999/11 \rfloor = 818$), and filtering those whose digit sum is divisible by $3$ leaves exactly $273$.

questions.source: Modified from 2022 HMMT November General Problem 2
questions.question: How many ways are there to arrange the numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ on the vertices of a regular pentagon such that exactly $2$ of the numbers are larger than both of their neighbors? Rotations and reflections are considered the same.
questions.solution: Brute-forcing all $5! = 120$ arrangements and identifying those with exactly two peaks (numbers exceeding both neighbors), then quotienting by the 10 symmetries of the pentagon, gives exactly $8$ arrangements.

questions.source: Modified from 2022 HMMT November Theme Problem 3
questions.question: Alice is bored in class, so she thinks of the number $2024$. Every second after that, she subtracts from her current number its smallest prime divisor (possibly itself). What is her number after $100$ seconds?
questions.solution: Iterating the process: starting from $2024$ and repeatedly subtracting the smallest prime factor ($2$ whenever the number is even), after exactly $100$ subtractions the value is $2024 - 200 = 1824$ (all 100 numbers along the way are even, so each subtraction removes exactly $2$).

questions.source: Modified from 2023 HMMT November General Problem 1
questions.question: Three people are playing rock-paper-scissors. They each play one of the three options independently at random, with equal probability. The probability that someone beats both of the other players is $\tfrac{m}{n}$ in lowest terms. Find $m+n$.
questions.solution: For a specific player, beating both others has probability $(1/3)^2 = 1/9$. The three players' events are disjoint (two people cannot both beat everyone), so the probability is $3 \cdot \frac19 = \frac13$, and $m+n = 1+3 = 4$.
